t: Sanxingdui was a Bronze Age culture in Sichuan, contemporary with the Shang dynasty, that cast bronzes in a style of its own: great masks with bulging eyes, a life-sized standing figure and a bronze tree almost 4 m high.
Its people built a walled city of 3.6 square kilometres, ringed by canals and divided into districts, and the culture is thought to have been governed by a strong central theocracy.
Many Chinese archaeologists identify it with the early kingdom of Shu, whose legendary founder Cancong was said to have protruding eyes like those of the bronze masks.
dyk: Paint survives on the bronze faces, black on the large eyes and eyebrows and vermilion on the lips, nostrils and ear holes, which the sinologist Corinne Debaine-Francfort reads as offerings for the head to taste, smell and hear.
ev: A walled city is founded at Sanxingdui on the banks of the Yazi River
The date radiocarbon dating gives the gold, bronze, jade and pottery objects later found in the sacrificial pits
The state of Qin conquers the region of the kingdom of Shu
A farmer dredging an irrigation ditch unearths a large cache of jade objects
David Crockett Graham of West China Union University organises the first archaeological excavation
Local workers find two sacrificial pits filled with broken and burned gold, bronze, jade and pottery objects
The Sanxingdui Museum opens near the site
Six more sacrificial pits are excavated, yielding a gold mask, ivory, bronzes and traces of silk

f.homeland: Sichuan, in south-west China, outside Chengdu. Key sites: Sanxingdui, about 4 km north-east of Nanxing Township in Guanghan (Deyang), on the Yazi River, and the related Jinsha site 40 km away.
f.period: Periods II–III of the Sanxingdui site, contemporary with the Shang dynasty; the walled city was founded c. 1600 BCE and the objects in the pits are radiocarbon-dated to the 12th–11th centuries BCE. Period I belongs to the Baodun culture.
f.known: bronze masks and heads with protruding eyes; the world’s oldest life-sized standing human statue; a bronze tree 3.96 m high with birds; gold masks; jade cong and zhang; sacrificial pits; a walled city of 3.6 square kilometres ringed by canals
f.sources: Chance finds from 1927 and excavations from 1934, above all the pits found in 1986 and 2020–2022; radiocarbon dating; much later Chinese texts on the kingdom of Shu (the Shiji, the Shujing, the Chronicles of Huayang). No written records of its own survive.
